stem: Which type annotation describes "a function that takes a number and returns a string"?

options.text: `(n: number) => string`
options.why: A function type expression names each parameter and gives the return type after the arrow.

options.text: `(number) => string`
options.why: This declares a parameter called `number` with no type. Under `strict` it is error TS7051.

options.text: `function (n: number): string`
options.why: That is the syntax of a function expression, not of a type, so it is not valid in a type position.

options.text: `Function<number, string>`
options.why: The global `Function` type is not generic, and it would accept any function anyway.

explanation: In a function type expression the parameter names are required, even though only the types matter for compatibility. Writing `(number) => string` is a classic slip: TypeScript reads `number` as a parameter name of type `any`, which `strict` rejects.

options.text: `string`
options.why: An optional parameter may be omitted, so TypeScript must allow for it being missing.

options.text: `string | undefined`
options.why: An optional parameter is `undefined` when the caller leaves it out, so `undefined` joins its type.

options.text: `string | null`
options.why: Omitted arguments are `undefined`, never `null`; `null` only appears if you add it.

options.text: `any`, because optional parameters stay untyped until checked
options.why: The parameter is annotated, so it keeps that type; `any` only appears for unannotated parameters.

explanation: Marking a parameter with `?` lets callers omit it, and inside the function its type becomes `T | undefined`. Narrow it (for example `title ?? "Dr"`) before using string methods on it.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: a default value makes the parameter optional for callers and supplies its type.

options.text: False
options.why: It is true: the default `3` gives the type `number`, and a defaulted parameter may be omitted.

explanation: A parameter with a default initializer is optional at call sites and is typed from the initializer. Inside the body it is plain `number`, not `number | undefined`, because the default fills in any missing value.

options.text: `sum()`
options.why: A rest parameter may receive zero arguments; `nums` is then an empty array.
Each argument becomes one element of `nums`, which is exactly what a rest parameter is for.
The array itself is a single argument, and `number[]` is not assignable to `number`.
Spreading the array passes its elements as separate number arguments, so this compiles.

explanation: A rest parameter `...nums: number[]` collects the remaining arguments into an array, and each argument must be a `number`. To pass an existing array, spread it: `sum(...values)`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Rest Parameters and Arguments

explanation: `readonly` properties may be initialised where they are declared or assigned in the constructor; any later assignment is a compile error. It is a type-level guarantee only and does not freeze the value at runtime.

stem: Match each class member modifier with what it allows.

options.text: Accessible from any code (the default)
options.why: Default visibility.

options.text: Accessible inside the class and its subclasses
options.why: Visibility for subclasses.

options.why: Class-only visibility.

explanation: Members are `public` unless you say otherwise. `protected` opens access to subclasses, `private` restricts it to the declaring class, and `readonly` controls writing rather than visibility, so it combines with the others (for example `private readonly id`).

stem: Which two are valid ways to write the type of a function that takes a string and returns a number? (Choose two.)

options.text: `(s: string) => number`
options.why: A function type expression is the usual, shortest form.

options.text: `{ (s: string): number }`
options.why: An object type with a call signature describes the same function and can also hold properties.

options.why: This names a parameter `string` with an implicit `any` type, which strict mode reports as TS7051.

options.text: `function (s: string): number`
options.why: That is expression syntax and is not allowed in a type position.

options.text: `Function`
options.why: The `Function` type accepts any function and makes every call return `any`.

explanation: Function type expressions and call signatures are interchangeable for plain functions. Use the call-signature form when the function also has properties, for example `{ (s: string): number; cacheSize: number }`.

stem: Put these lines of an overloaded function in the order TypeScript expects, so that the most specific overload is tried first.

options.text: `function parse(input: "json"): object;`
options.why: The most specific overload.

options.text: `function parse(input: string): string;`
options.why: The general overload.

options.text: `function parse(input: string): object | string { /* ... */ }`
options.why: The implementation, which must come last.

explanation: Overload signatures are listed first and the implementation comes immediately after them. TypeScript picks the first overload that matches a call, so put specific overloads (like the literal `"json"`) before general ones; otherwise the general one would match first and hide them.

explanation: A contextual function type with a `void` return accepts functions that return anything, which is what lets you write `arr.forEach(x => list.push(x))` even though `push` returns a number. Callers see the result as `void` and should not use it. (At runtime `result` is in fact 42.)

Which two lines are compile errors? (Choose two.)

```ts
type Cb = () => void;                       // line 1
const a: Cb = () => 42;                     // line 2
function b(): void { return 42; }           // line 3
const c: number = a();                      // line 4
const d: Cb = function () { return "ok"; }; // line 5
```

options.why: A type alias for a function type is always fine.

options.text: Line 2
options.why: A `void` function type accepts a function that returns a value.

options.text: Line 3
options.why: A function declared with a `void` return type may not return a value (TS2322).

options.text: Line 4
options.why: Calling a `Cb` produces `void`, which is not assignable to `number`.

options.text: Line 5
options.why: Like line 2, a function expression assigned to a void function type may return anything.

explanation: The leniency applies only when a function is checked against a void function type (lines 2 and 5). A function whose own declared return type is `void` must not return a value (line 3), and the result of calling a void function type is `void`, which can't be used as a number (line 4).
reference: TypeScript FAQ: Why are functions returning non-void assignable to function returning void?

options.why: Each overload is tried on its own, and a union argument fits neither, so the union needs its own signature.

options.why: Overload resolution never merges signatures; it checks each one separately and needs one to match fully.

options.why: The overloads each take one argument; the problem is the argument's type, not the count.

explanation: Callers only see overload signatures, and TypeScript resolves a call against them one at a time. A `string | number[]` argument matches neither. The handbook advice is: prefer a union parameter over overloads when the return type does not depend on the input, as here: `function len(x: string | any[]): number`.

stem:
Under `strict`, which statement is true?

```ts
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
nums.forEach((n) => n.toFixed(1)); // line 2
const double = (n) => n * 2;       // line 3
```

options.text: Both lines error, because neither callback annotates `n`
options.why: Line 2's callback gets its parameter type from `forEach`, so it needs no annotation.

options.text: Neither line errors, because TypeScript infers `number` from the `* 2`
options.why: TypeScript does not infer parameter types from how the body uses them.

options.text: Only line 3 errors: `n` implicitly has an `any` type
options.why: Line 3 has no contextual type to borrow, so `n` would be `any`, which `noImplicitAny` rejects.

options.why: The callback's return value is ignored, and void callbacks may return anything.

explanation: Contextual typing gives a callback its parameter types from where it is passed: `forEach` says the callback receives a `number`. A standalone arrow function has no context, so its parameters must be annotated, as in `(n: number) => n * 2`.

options.text: True

options.why: Correct: `implements` does not contextually type members, so `other` is an implicit `any` (TS7006 under strict).

explanation: An `implements` clause is a check: TypeScript verifies that the class is assignable to the interface, but it does not change the class's type or flow types into its members. Annotate `other: number` yourself.

stem: Under `strict`, `class User { name: string; }` reports "Property 'name' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor". Which three changes remove the error? (Choose three.)

options.text: Give it an initializer: `name: string = "";`
options.why: An initializer guarantees the property is set when the object is created.

options.text: Add a definite assignment assertion: `name!: string;`
options.why: `!` tells the compiler you guarantee initialisation some other way, and it stops checking.

options.text: Assign it in the constructor: `constructor() { this.name = "anon"; }`
options.why: Assignment in the constructor body is exactly what the check looks for.

options.text: Mark it `readonly name: string;`
options.why: `readonly` restricts later writes; it does nothing to guarantee a first value.

options.text: Assign it in a method `init()` that the constructor calls
options.why: The check only analyses the constructor body itself, not methods it calls.

explanation: `strictPropertyInitialization` checks that every non-optional property is set by its initializer or by assignments in the constructor body. Other ways to satisfy it are making the property optional (`name?: string`) or adding `undefined` to its type. Reach for `!` only when something outside TypeScript's view, such as a framework, sets the value.

options.why: Correct: `C` only has what it declares, so `new C().p` is error TS2339.

explanation: Optional interface members are a common surprise: a class that implements the interface is valid without `p`, but `implements` does not merge the interface into the class type. Declare `p?: number` in the class too, or use declaration merging (`interface C extends I {}`) if you really want the members added.

options.text: `1 | 2`, because TypeScript resolves each member of the union separately
options.why: Overload resolution does not distribute over a union argument.

options.text: `number`, because only the `string` overload accepts the whole union
options.why: Neither literal overload accepts `"a" | "b"` on its own, so resolution falls through to the general one.

options.text: `1`, because the first overload matches the first member of the union
options.why: An overload must accept the whole argument type, not just one member of it.

options.text: A compile error: no overload matches
options.why: The final `string` overload accepts `"a" | "b"`, so the call compiles.

explanation: Overloads are checked one at a time against the argument as a whole. A union of literals matches neither literal overload, so the general `(x: string): number` signature is chosen and the precise information is lost. If you need `1 | 2` back, use a generic with a conditional or lookup type, for example `function pick<K extends "a" | "b">(x: K): { a: 1; b: 2 }[K]`.

options.text: Compile error: a method with a `this: Counter` parameter can't be assigned to `() => void`
options.why: tsc 6 accepts this assignment; the `this` parameter is only checked when the function is called with its own type.

options.text: It compiles and increments `c.n`, because `this` was bound at the assignment
options.why: Reading `c.inc` does not bind anything; `later()` is a plain call with no receiver.

options.text: It compiles, then throws a `TypeError` because `this` is `undefined` inside `inc`
options.why: The assignment is accepted, and the detached call runs `this.n++` on `undefined`.

options.text: It compiles and silently increments `globalThis.n`
options.why: Class bodies are always strict mode, so `this` is `undefined`, not the global object.

explanation: A `this` parameter is checked when you call the function through its own type (`c.inc()` is fine, `(0, c.inc)()` is not). Assigning the method to a function type without a `this` declaration is allowed, so the bug only shows up at runtime. Bind the method (`c.inc.bind(c)`), wrap it (`() => c.inc()`), or define it as an arrow-function property.

options.text: `[number, string]`
options.why: The tuple keeps the parameter labels, and the second element is optional.

options.text: `[x: number]`, because only parameter properties count
options.why: Every constructor parameter appears in the tuple, whether or not it becomes a property.

options.text: `[x: number, y?: string]`
options.why: Labels and optionality come straight from the constructor's parameter list.

options.text: `{ x: number; y?: string }`
options.why: `ConstructorParameters` produces a tuple, not an object type.

explanation: `ConstructorParameters` reads the constructor's signature: parameter properties count like any other parameter, labels are kept, and optional parameters become optional tuple elements (`y?: string`, which also admits `undefined` unless `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is on). This is handy for writing factories: `function create(...args: ConstructorParameters<typeof Point>) { return new Point(...args); }`.

stem: In TypeScript 5+ with no `experimentalDecorators` flag, which use of a decorator is a compile error?

options.text: A method decorator such as `@logged run() {}`
options.why: Method decorators are part of the standard proposal that TypeScript 5 implements.

options.text: A class decorator such as `@sealed class Service {}`
options.why: Class decorators are standard and need no flag.

options.text: A parameter decorator such as `go(@inject x: Token) {}`
options.why: Standard decorators can't decorate parameters, so TypeScript reports "Decorators are not valid here".

options.text: A decorator on an `accessor` field such as `@observable accessor value = 0`
options.why: Auto-accessors are part of the standard proposal and work without the flag.

explanation: TypeScript 5 implements the TC39 standard decorators for classes, methods, getters, setters, fields and auto-accessors, with a `context` object as the second argument. Parameter decorators and `emitDecoratorMetadata` belong to the older `experimentalDecorators` model, which frameworks like Angular and NestJS still rely on.

options.text: Both compile, and both subclasses report `name` as `"base"`
options.why: Under define semantics a redeclared field in `D1` becomes a real field that resets the value.

options.text: `D1` errors with TS2612; if emitted anyway, `new D1().name` is `undefined` while `new D2().name` is `"base"`
options.why: A redeclared field is re-initialised to `undefined` after `super()`, whereas `declare` emits nothing.

options.text: `D2` errors, because `declare` is only allowed in `.d.ts` files
options.why: `declare` on a class field is valid in normal files; it means "type only, emit nothing".

options.text: Both compile, and `!` makes `D1` copy the base value
options.why: `!` only switches off the definite-assignment check; it has no runtime effect.

explanation: With `useDefineForClassFields` (the default for ES2022 targets), every field written in a class body, even one without an initializer, is emitted and defined as `undefined` after `super()`, overwriting the base value. TypeScript catches this with TS2612 and suggests `declare`, which narrows the type without emitting a field.
reference: TypeScript 3.7 release notes: The useDefineForClassFields Flag and the declare Property Modifier

options.text: It logs `impl`, and TypeScript reports nothing
options.why: The base constructor runs before `Impl`'s field initializers, so `label` is not set yet.

options.text: TypeScript reports that an abstract method can't be called in a constructor
options.why: TypeScript has no such check; this pattern compiles cleanly.

options.text: It logs `undefined`, and TypeScript reports nothing
options.why: The override runs during `super()`, before `label = "impl"` has been initialised.

options.text: It throws a `TypeError`, because `describe` is abstract at runtime
options.why: At runtime the overridden `describe` from `Impl` exists and is called normally.

explanation: Calling an overridable method from a base constructor is unsafe in any language with this construction order. The subclass's override runs while the subclass's fields are still uninitialised, and the type system can't see it, since `label` is typed `string` but is `undefined` at that moment. Move the call out of the constructor, or pass the data to `super()`.
reference: MDN: Classes (constructor and field initialization order)

options.text: With `target: "ES2022"` it is error TS2729, but with `target: "ES2017"` it compiles and `doubled` is 10 for `new Money(5)`
options.why: Define semantics initialise fields before parameter properties are assigned; the older emit assigns parameters first.

options.text: It compiles for every target and always gives 10
options.why: Under ES2022 semantics `amount` is not yet set when `doubled` initialises, and TypeScript catches that.

options.text: It compiles for every target, but `doubled` is always `NaN` at runtime
options.why: With the older emit (`useDefineForClassFields: false`), parameter properties are assigned first, so it works.

options.text: It is always an error, because parameter properties can't be used in class fields
options.why: This is allowed with the older emit; only define semantics make the order unsafe.

explanation: The meaning of this class depends on `useDefineForClassFields`. With ES2022 targets it defaults to true and fields are native class fields, which are initialised before the constructor body assigns `this.amount`. TypeScript reports TS2729 "Property 'amount' is used before its initialization". With older targets the field initializer is moved into the constructor after the parameter assignments. Assign `doubled` in the constructor to be safe either way.

stem: Which two statements about function overloads are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Callers cannot see the implementation signature; only the overload signatures can be called
options.why: The implementation signature is there to check the body, not to be called.

options.text: Each overload must be compatible with the implementation, so `(x: number): number` breaks if the implementation returns only `string`
options.why: TypeScript reports TS2394 when an overload is not compatible with its implementation.

options.text: TypeScript chooses the best-fitting overload no matter what order they are declared in
options.why: Resolution takes the first matching overload in declaration order.

options.text: A union-typed argument is resolved by combining several overloads
options.why: Each overload is checked on its own; a union needs one signature that accepts all of it.

options.text: Each overload is emitted as a separate JavaScript function
options.why: Overload signatures are erased; only the single implementation is emitted.

explanation: Overloads are a type-level view over one JavaScript function. The implementation must handle every overload (its parameters must accept theirs, and its return type must be compatible with each). Callers see only the overloads, tried in order. If the implementation's return type doesn't cover an overload, you get TS2394 "This overload signature is not compatible with its implementation signature".
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Overload Signatures and the Implementation Signature

options.text: Nothing: `*` always produces a number, so the return type is inferred as `number`
options.why: To type `n * fact(n - 1)` TypeScript first needs the return type of `fact`, which is the very thing it is inferring.

options.text: TS7023: `fact` implicitly has return type `any`, because it is referenced in its own return expression
options.why: Inference hits a cycle, so it falls back to `any`, which `noImplicitAny` reports.

options.text: Nothing: the return type is inferred as `1 | number`, which simplifies to `number`
options.why: Inference never gets that far, because of the cycle through `fact` itself.

options.text: A compile-time error about possible infinite recursion
options.why: TypeScript does not analyse whether recursion terminates.

explanation: Return-type inference can't use the function's own return type, so a function that recurses in its return expression gets an implicit `any`, which strict mode reports as TS7023. Annotating the return type (`function fact(n: number): number`) fixes it, and is good practice for recursive and exported functions anyway.

options.text: `eval A`
options.why: The first decorator expression is evaluated first.

options.text: `eval B`
options.why: Expressions are evaluated from top (left) to bottom (right).

options.text: `apply B`
options.why: The decorator closest to the method is applied first.

options.text: `apply A`
options.why: The outermost decorator is applied last.

explanation: Decorator expressions are evaluated in source order, top to bottom, and the resulting decorators are applied in reverse, innermost first, like function composition: `A(B(run))`. This is the same for standard and legacy decorators. It matters when one decorator wraps the result of another, for example logging around caching.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Decorator Composition; TC39 decorators proposal
